Precious Metals Quarterly 2011 Q2 

# Executive summary 

## Gold: a final leg of the bull run is still possible 

After eight consecutive years of surplus, the gold market was again in oversupply in 2010 by 1,420 tonnes.  This is 4.5% higher than in 2009, and is thanks to increased mine output and ample scrap supplies while the recovery in fabrication demand was moderate. 



- We expect total fabrication demand for gold to fully recover by 2015 and exceed that experienced in 2007 before the effects of the financial crisis took hold.  2015 offtake could perhaps even challenge the previous peak recorded 1997. 



- In the jewellery sector, India and China will remain key and growing markets.  However, there are many other emerging countries across Asia and the Middle East that share an historical, cultural, and even religious affinity to gold as a traditional monetary medium for saving and investment.  As many of these countries prosper and as the wealth of their citizens increases, they are likely to demand more gold in the form of jewellery too. 



- Against this, gold fabrication for other applications will grow more slowly alongside an economic recovery that is held back by consumers’ need to allocate a higher share of their incomes to savings and debt repayments. 



- Gold supply might increase by no more than a net 3.7% between 2010 and 2015.  Mine production is forecast to grow by almost 17%, but scrap recovery could decline by 24%. 



- Investment in gold in various forms is expected to keep rising over the next 12-18 months supported by global economic uncertainty, heightened by sovereign debt risk, rising inflationary pressure, low interest rates, and investment diversification.  In 2014 and 2015, however, when global economic recovery is anticipated to get a firmer footing and some major concerns have tapered out, investors might decide that the gold price is becoming vulnerable to a decline and start reducing the weight of gold in their holdings. 



- We expect the gold price to pause around current levels for a while such that it averages $1,460/oz in 2011.  However, a renewed rally toward perhaps $1,600/oz next year could put the 2012 average at a real $1,525/oz.  This will be driven by jewellery demand picking up in the developing countries, net buying by the official sector and anti-inflation hedging. 



- In late 2012 or early 2013, however, we expect the gold price rally to halt as global economic conditions normalise and a sustained rise in interest rates makes other investments more attractive.  Overall, the average gold price over the 2011-15 period is thus expected to equal $1,479/oz in nominal terms and $1,430 in real terms.

## Other precious metal markets 

#### Silver 

The rally to almost $50/oz proved that silver has the potential to appreciate relative to gold to the extent that the gold-silver price ratio drops

to almost 30.  A sharp decrease in ETF holdings also shows that investors are willing to pull out of silver as much as pile in.  Our forecast again assumes that investors’ interest in gold and silver will push quotations higher through 2012. 



- Elevated prices are making almost the entire universe of mine projects attractive and so supply growth should largely been unencumbered.  Although global mine supply will not grow in 2011, more ventures are now committed than there were three months ago, and we forecast annual output increasing by more than 2,800 tonnes in 2010-15 to 26,850 tonnes. 



- Fabrication will also grow.  We have raised our historical estimates of offtake in China to the extent that the global total now surpasses its 2000 peak as early as 2012.  After running at 5,000 t/y in 2009-10, the global metal surplus will therefore run at 3,500 t/y so long as the economic recovery continues.  Of course, sharply lower prices will trim the surplus further. 

#### Platinum 

Although we still expect platinum’s fundamental surplus to narrow in 2011, this may no longer be at quite our previously anticipated rate.  And 2013 might now be the first year in which investors need to destock in order to balance the market. 



- The Japanese earthquake has had two effects on platinum demand, one temporary and one perhaps longer-lasting.  Disruptions to vehicle production (and hence autocatalyst use) should be made up in the second half of 2011.  However, lower jewellery offtake as discretionary spending is curtailed could continue into 2012 and 2013. 



- Consumption loses have so far had more effect than production disruptions in South Africa, the latter stemming mainly from safety issues. 



- However, investment has been strong enough to absorb this unexpected metal, and our price forecast is largely unchanged. 

#### Palladium 

For the first time since 2005, palladium fabrication now appears to have exceeded mine and scrap supply in 2010, while surging Russian sales were more than absorbed by the growth in ETFs.  However, 2011 and 2012 are still likely to see a return to surplus before deficits grow more sustainably only from 2013. 



- Since cars there are largely petrol-engined, palladium is more exposed than platinum to the weaker Japanese vehicle market. 

- Increased scrap availability is meanwhile boosting this year’s supply. 



- ETF holdings have also slipped a little (although they could still grow in 2011 overall).

## Data sources and study team 

The historical data presented in this report are based on estimates published by a variety of sources, including Johnson Matthey (JM), World Gold Council (WGC), International Financial Statistics (IFS), JD Power, London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), CPM, GTIS trade statistics, company websites and written reports. 

However, CRU’s interpretation of the data may or may not coincide with those expressed in these various sources. 

The forecast is exclusively CRU’s.
